components.gap: Lauritzen's Definition 2.47 (p. 66, inside the locator 'Propositions 2.46-2.48' of body lines 6-8, whose shared numbering spans Definition 2.47, and inside pp. 65-68) defines the Bayesian network (D,P) generated by D and the adapted kernels as their recursive combination P. components.gap: Theorem 1.28's proof (pp. 19-20) carries the source's justification for its construction: quantile functions are not unique, and although each is increasing and hence measurable, the various choices may destroy joint measurability, so the key is to remove the choices with an operationally defined quantile that singles out the largest p-quantile. The handbook proof (annex 199-244) adopts 'the source's upper quantile' and proves joint measurability, but nowhere states that separate quantile choices for different parameter values can fail to be jointly measurable, the reason the operational choice is needed. (The converse relation to the equations-to-kernels direction is reported at annex 314-316.)

components.gap: Lauritzen introduces Theorem 2.44 with the claim (p. 65) that, in contrast to the undirected case, the directed global, local and ordered Markov properties are all equivalent without further regularity assumptions. The handbook states the absence of regularity hypotheses (body 125-126, 209-211; no intersection axiom, positivity or density) but nowhere states the contrast with undirected graphs, whose corresponding properties need further assumptions; no undirected Markov property appears on the route. Also unreported is the p. 68 statement, on the cited page range, that when such a network has a density with respect to a product measure 'the results above can be strengthened'; body 5-8 says only that the source treats densities separately.
